Continuity and Differentiability — JEE Main revision guide

Continuity asks whether the graph reaches the assigned height. Differentiability asks whether there is one finite slope there. Continuity of the derivative asks a third question: do nearby slopes approach that slope?

Scope and source difficulties before studying

The official Mathematics Unit 7 includes continuity, differentiability, algebraic/composite/implicit differentiation, and derivatives up to order two. This chapter teaches those tools. The separate Applications of Derivatives chapter is not being started.

  • Q34 has inconsistent data. The functional equation and f′(0)=3f'(0)=3f′(0)=3 force f(x)=e3xf(x)=e^{3x}f(x)=e3x, which contradicts the printed f(5)=2f(5)=2f(5)=2. The intended formal calculation gives 666, but there is no function satisfying all the givens. The worked solution explains both facts.
  • Rolle's and Lagrange's mean value theorems are source extensions. They are not named in the current official syllabus. We retain Q7, Q8, Q26 and Q31 and teach the conditions, but do not call those theorems new core exam requirements.
  • Q35 needs a≠0a\ne0a=0 for a parametric curve with a defined slope. For a=0a=0a=0 the point does not move.
  • Q5 and Q30 need their principal inverse-trig branches. Their interval restrictions are part of the solution.
  • Q29 has a local log domain. Its real inputs lie in (−1/2,1/3)(-1/2,1/3)(−1/2,1/3), with the value at zero filled separately.

Formula and concept bank

Concept C01 — Continuity: left height, right height and actual value

At an interior point aaa, continuity means

lim⁡x→a−f(x)=lim⁡x→a+f(x)=f(a).\boxed{\lim_{x\to a^-}f(x)=\lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)=f(a)}.x→a−lim​f(x)=x→a+lim​f(x)=f(a)​.

The three jobs are different:

  1. Find the height approached from the left.
  2. Find the height approached from the right.
  3. Check the actual assigned value at aaa.

A limit existing is not enough if the assigned value is wrong. A function being defined at aaa is not enough if the nearby heights disagree.

Read the picture: a hollow point marks the missing value before filling. Put a filled point at that same height to obtain continuity.

Important for JEE Main: piecewise parameter questions usually start with this three-way match. Each formula may be continuous on its own piece; the joins need checking.

Polynomials are continuous everywhere. Rational functions are continuous where their denominator is nonzero. Sine, cosine and exponentials are continuous everywhere; logarithms, roots, tangent and inverse functions must respect their domains. Sums, products and compositions of continuous functions remain continuous where defined; a quotient also needs a nonzero denominator.

At a closed-domain endpoint, continuity uses the available side. Always say whether the question asks about a function on all real inputs or on a smaller natural domain.

Useful discontinuity types:

  • Removable: a finite limit exists, but the point value is missing or wrong. One correct filled value repairs it.
  • Jump: the two finite side limits differ. Changing one point value cannot repair it.
  • Infinite or oscillating: there is no finite nearby height to fill.

Concept C02 — Differentiability means one finite slope

The derivative at aaa is

f′(a)=lim⁡h→0f(a+h)−f(a)h\boxed{f'(a)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}h}f′(a)=h→0lim​hf(a+h)−f(a)​​

when this limit is a finite real number. The quotient is output change divided by input change: a nearby secant slope. As the second point moves in, it approaches the tangent slope.

Define the left and right derivatives using h→0−h\to0^-h→0− and h→0+h\to0^+h→0+ in this same expression. The denominator is still hhh; a left-hand increment is negative.

For f(x)=∣x∣f(x)=|x|f(x)=∣x∣ at zero,

f(h)−f(0)h=∣h∣h={−1,h<0,1,h>0.\frac{f(h)-f(0)}h=\frac{|h|}{h} =\begin{cases}-1,&h<0,\\1,&h>0.\end{cases}hf(h)−f(0)​=h∣h∣​={−1,1,​h<0,h>0.​

The graph reaches the same height from both sides, but the slopes differ:

∣x∣ is continuous at 0 but not differentiable there.\boxed{|x|\text{ is continuous at }0 \text{ but not differentiable there}.}∣x∣ is continuous at 0 but not differentiable there.​

Read the picture: there is no height gap. There is a corner, so no single tangent slope.

Differentiability implies continuity. If the difference quotient tends to mmm, then

f(a+h)−f(a)=h f(a+h)−f(a)h⟶0⋅m=0.f(a+h)-f(a) =h\,\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}h\longrightarrow0\cdot m=0.f(a+h)−f(a)=hhf(a+h)−f(a)​⟶0⋅m=0.

So nearby values approach f(a)f(a)f(a). The converse is false, as ∣x∣|x|∣x∣ shows.

For a piecewise join: match the value first. Then compare slopes. If the pieces have derivatives extending to the join and the function is continuous there, these side derivative values can be used. Otherwise return to the difference-quotient definition.

A vertical tangent is another warning: for x1/3x^{1/3}x1/3 at zero, the quotient is 1/h2/3→+∞1/h^{2/3}\to+\infty1/h2/3→+∞. The graph is continuous, but there is no finite derivative. A cusp can have opposite infinite slopes. “It looks joined” is therefore not a derivative test.

Concept C03 — Algebra rules and the standard limits used here

Let u=u(x)u=u(x)u=u(x) and v=v(x)v=v(x)v=v(x) be differentiable at the input in question:

(cu+dv)′=cu′+dv′,(uv)′=u′v+uv′,\boxed{(cu+dv)'=cu'+dv'},\qquad \boxed{(uv)'=u'v+uv'},(cu+dv)′=cu′+dv′​,(uv)′=u′v+uv′​, (uv)′=u′v−uv′v2(v≠0).\boxed{\left(\frac uv\right)'=\frac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}} \quad(v\ne0).(vu​)′=v2u′v−uv′​​(v=0).

c,dc,dc,d are constants. A constant's derivative is zero. For an integer power, (xn)′=nxn−1(x^n)'=nx^{n-1}(xn)′=nxn−1 wherever the function is defined; for a general real exponent, use the positive-input branch unless a larger real domain is justified.

Why two product terms? When both factors change, one first-order contribution comes from the change in uuu, the other from the change in vvv. Their small-change product is of higher order. Differentiating both factors and multiplying, u′v′u'v'u′v′, misses the main contributions.

For example,

(x2ln⁡x)′=2xln⁡x+x21x=2xln⁡x+x(x>0).(x^2\ln x)'=2x\ln x+x^2\frac1x =2x\ln x+x\quad(x>0).(x2lnx)′=2xlnx+x2x1​=2xlnx+x(x>0).

Simplify first when it saves work. For x2/x=xx^2/x=xx2/x=x away from zero, cancel before differentiating. But cancellation does not automatically define the original quotient at zero.

The supplied limit questions also use these radian results:

sin⁡tt→1,tan⁡tt→1,1−cos⁡tt2→12,et−1t→1,ln⁡(1+t)t→1.\frac{\sin t}{t}\to1,\quad \frac{\tan t}{t}\to1,\quad \frac{1-\cos t}{t^2}\to\frac12,\quad \frac{e^t-1}{t}\to1,\quad \frac{\ln(1+t)}t\to1.tsint​→1,ttant​→1,t21−cost​→21​,tet−1​→1,tln(1+t)​→1.

They are limits as t→0t\to0t→0 within the real domain. Useful local expansions are

et=1+t+t2/2+O(t3),sin⁡t=t−t3/6+O(t5),cos⁡t=1−t2/2+O(t4),e^t=1+t+t^2/2+O(t^3),\quad \sin t=t-t^3/6+O(t^5),\quad \cos t=1-t^2/2+O(t^4),et=1+t+t2/2+O(t3),sint=t−t3/6+O(t5),cost=1−t2/2+O(t4), ln⁡(1+t)=t−t2/2+O(t3).\ln(1+t)=t-t^2/2+O(t^3).ln(1+t)=t−t2/2+O(t3).

O(tm)O(t^m)O(tm) is a remainder bounded by a fixed constant times ∣t∣m|t|^m∣t∣m nearby. These expansions describe the first surviving terms; they are not exact equalities without their remainders.

Concept C04 — Chain rule: outside change times inside change

If y=F(u(x))y=F(u(x))y=F(u(x)), then

dydx=F′(u(x))u′(x).\boxed{\frac{dy}{dx}=F'(u(x))u'(x)}.dxdy​=F′(u(x))u′(x)​.

The input first changes uuu; that change then changes FFF. The two rates multiply. For example,

ddxsin⁡(x2)=cos⁡(x2) (2x),\frac d{dx}\sin(x^2)=\cos(x^2)\,(2x),dxd​sin(x2)=cos(x2)(2x),

not just cos⁡(x2)\cos(x^2)cos(x2). Point to the inside expression before differentiating.

sin⁡−1z\sin^{-1}zsin−1z returns its principal angle in [−π/2,π/2][-\pi/2,\pi/2][−π/2,π/2]. Thus

sin⁡−1(sin⁡t)=t only when −π/2≤t≤π/2.\boxed{\sin^{-1}(\sin t)=t\ \text{only when }-\pi/2\le t\le\pi/2.}sin−1(sint)=t only when −π/2≤t≤π/2.​

Concept C06 — Modulus and floor: inspect the special inputs

For u(x)≠0u(x)\ne0u(x)=0,

(∣u∣)′=u∣u∣u′.\boxed{(|u|)'=\frac{u}{|u|}u'}.(∣u∣)′=∣u∣u​u′​.

At u(a)=0u(a)=0u(a)=0, this formula is undefined. Check the original difference quotient or the local expression.

For ∣x−c∣|x-c|∣x−c∣, the derivative is −1-1−1 before ccc and 111 after ccc. It jumps by 222. In a sum of positively weighted modulus terms, a single zero of one term gives a genuine new corner because the other nonzero terms are smooth there.

A multiplier can remove a corner. With h=x−ah=x-ah=x−a,

∣h∣: corner,h∣h∣: h∣h∣−0h=∣h∣→0.|h|:\ \text{corner},\qquad h|h|:\ \frac{h|h|-0}{h}=|h|\to0.∣h∣: corner,h∣h∣: hh∣h∣−0​=∣h∣→0.

So h∣h∣h|h|h∣h∣ is differentiable at zero. Also, if differentiable uuu has u(a)=u′(a)=0u(a)=u'(a)=0u(a)=u′(a)=0, then ∣u∣|u|∣u∣ is differentiable there with derivative zero. Merely counting roots inside a modulus can overcount.

For the floor function,

[t]=⌊t⌋,t−1<[t]≤t.[t]=\lfloor t\rfloor,\quad t-1<[t]\le t.[t]=⌊t⌋,t−1<[t]≤t.

It jumps at each integer and is constant between consecutive integers. For [3x][3x][3x], solve 3x=m3x=m3x=m for integer mmm and check the requested interval. At a floor boundary, inspect the sides; touching a level without crossing it need not produce the same jump as a strictly increasing argument.

For example, [x2][x^2][x2] is zero throughout a small neighbourhood of zero, so it is continuous there. But [−x2][-x^2][−x2] is −1-1−1 at nearby nonzero inputs and 000 at zero, so it is discontinuous there. In both examples the inside reaches an integer at zero; the side values decide what actually happens.

For sin⁡∣x∣\sin|x|sin∣x∣ and ∣sin⁡x∣|\sin x|∣sinx∣, both functions equal ∣sin⁡x∣|\sin x|∣sinx∣ sufficiently close to zero, so both have a corner there. They are not equal everywhere: for π<∣x∣<2π\pi<|x|<2\piπ<∣x∣<2π, sin⁡∣x∣\sin|x|sin∣x∣ can be negative while ∣sin⁡x∣|\sin x|∣sinx∣ cannot.

Concept C07 — Oscillation: check the function and derivative separately

Define

f(x)=xsin⁡(1/x),g(x)=x2sin⁡(1/x)(x≠0),f(0)=g(0)=0.f(x)=x\sin(1/x),\quad g(x)=x^2\sin(1/x)\quad(x\ne0),\qquad f(0)=g(0)=0.f(x)=xsin(1/x),g(x)=x2sin(1/x)(x=0),f(0)=g(0)=0.

Both are continuous at zero because ∣f(x)∣≤∣x∣|f(x)|\le|x|∣f(x)∣≤∣x∣ and ∣g(x)∣≤x2|g(x)|\le x^2∣g(x)∣≤x2. But their derivative quotients are different:

Therefore f′(0)f'(0)f′(0) does not exist, while g′(0)=0g'(0)=0g′(0)=0.

For x≠0x\ne0x=0,

g′(x)=2xsin⁡(1/x)−cos⁡(1/x).g'(x)=2x\sin(1/x)-\cos(1/x).g′(x)=2xsin(1/x)−cos(1/x).

Its first term tends to zero, but the cosine term continues to oscillate with size one. Along xn=1/(2πn)x_n=1/(2\pi n)xn​=1/(2πn), g′(xn)=−1g'(x_n)=-1g′(xn​)=−1; along yn=1/((2n+1)π)y_n=1/((2n+1)\pi)yn​=1/((2n+1)π), g′(yn)=1g'(y_n)=1g′(yn​)=1. Thus g′g'g′ is not continuous at zero.

Read the panels: small function height does not guarantee settling slopes.

Important for JEE Main: distinguish fff continuous, fff differentiable, and f′f'f′ continuous. The last is stronger than the second.

For awareness, multiplying by still more powers can tame the derivative too. For example, x3sin⁡(1/x)x^3\sin(1/x)x3sin(1/x) extended by zero has derivative 3x2sin⁡(1/x)−xcos⁡(1/x)→03x^2\sin(1/x)-x\cos(1/x)\to03x2sin(1/x)−xcos(1/x)→0. Concept C08 — Logarithmic differentiation for variable powers

For y=u(x)v(x)y=u(x)^{v(x)}y=u(x)v(x) with u>0u>0u>0, take the logarithm:

ln⁡y=vln⁡u.\ln y=v\ln u.lny=vlnu.

Differentiate using the product and chain rules:

y′=uv(v′ln⁡u+v u′u).\boxed{y'=u^v\left(v'\ln u+v\,\frac{u'}u\right)}.y′=uv(v′lnu+vuu′​)​.

There are two contributions: change in the exponent and change in the base. The ordinary rule d(xn)/dx=nxn−1d(x^n)/dx=nx^{n-1}d(xn)/dx=nxn−1 assumes a constant exponent. Applying it to xxx^xxx would miss the exponent's change.

For y=xxy=x^xy=xx with x>0x>0x>0,

ln⁡y=xln⁡x,y′y=ln⁡x+1,y′=xx(1+ln⁡x).\ln y=x\ln x,\quad \frac{y'}y=\ln x+1,\quad \boxed{y'=x^x(1+\ln x)}.lny=xlnx,yy′​=lnx+1,y′=xx(1+lnx)​.

For y=xsin⁡xy=x^{\sin x}y=xsinx with x>0x>0x>0,

y′=xsin⁡x(cos⁡xln⁡x+sin⁡xx).\boxed{y'=x^{\sin x}\left(\cos x\ln x+\frac{\sin x}{x}\right)}.y′=xsinx(cosxlnx+xsinx​)​.

Differentiate before substituting the input. Substituting x=π/2x=\pi/2x=π/2 at the start turns the function into one number; a number does not retain information about nearby change.

Logs also turn long nonzero products and quotients into sums and differences. Use ln⁡∣y∣\ln|y|ln∣y∣ where a nonzero function is negative and the identity is valid locally; do not take a real ln⁡y\ln ylny of a negative value.

For the supplied power limit,

Y=(cos⁡x)1/x2,ln⁡Y=ln⁡cos⁡xx2→−12,Y→e−1/2.Y=(\cos x)^{1/x^2},\quad \ln Y=\frac{\ln\cos x}{x^2}\to-\frac12, \quad \boxed{Y\to e^{-1/2}}.Y=(cosx)1/x2,lnY=x2lncosx​→−21​,Y→e−1/2​.

Here cos⁡x>0\cos x>0cosx>0 sufficiently near zero. One way to check the log limit is to write u=cos⁡x−1u=\cos x-1u=cosx−1, use ln⁡(1+u)/u→1\ln(1+u)/u\to1ln(1+u)/u→1, and u/x2→−1/2u/x^2\to-1/2u/x2→−1/2.

Concept C09 — Implicit and parametric derivatives

Implicit means x,yx,yx,y are linked by an equation instead of yyy being isolated. Treat yyy as a changing function of xxx:

x2+y2=r2⇒2x+2y y′=0⇒y′=−x/y(y≠0).x^2+y^2=r^2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad2x+2y\,y'=0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \boxed{y'=-x/y}\quad(y\ne0).x2+y2=r2⇒2x+2yy′=0⇒y′=−x/y​(y=0).

Why the extra y′y'y′? Differentiating y2y^2y2 uses the chain rule. At y=0y=0y=0 we cannot divide by yyy; the circle has a vertical tangent there, not a finite slope.

Read the picture: the radius has slope 4/34/34/3 and the tangent has slope −3/4-3/4−3/4, so their product is −1-1−1. The derivative calculation agrees with the geometry.

More generally, for differentiable F(x,y)=0F(x,y)=0F(x,y)=0 locally defining yyy,

y′=−Fx/Fy(Fy≠0).\boxed{y'=-F_x/F_y}\quad(F_y\ne0).y′=−Fx​/Fy​​(Fy​=0).

FxF_xFx​ means differentiate with respect to xxx while holding yyy fixed; FyF_yFy​ means the reverse. This is a compact form of the same implicit calculation, not an extra condition to memorize without meaning.

Parametric means a third input ttt controls both coordinates:

x=X(t),y=Y(t).x=X(t),\qquad y=Y(t).x=X(t),y=Y(t).

Provided X′(t)≠0X'(t)\ne0X′(t)=0,

dydx=dy/dtdx/dt.\boxed{\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}}.dxdy​=dx/dtdy/dt​​.

Both numerator and denominator are changes per unit ttt; dividing them gives change in yyy per unit xxx.

For the second derivative, differentiate that slope with respect to xxx, not merely to ttt:

d2ydx2=ddt(dy/dx) 1dx/dt=Y′′X′−Y′X′′(X′)3.\boxed{\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} =\frac{d}{dt}(dy/dx)\,\frac1{dx/dt} =\frac{Y''X'-Y'X''}{(X')^3}}.dx2d2y​=dtd​(dy/dx)dx/dt1​=(X′)3Y′′X′−Y′X′′​​.

If X′=0X'=0X′=0, stop and inspect the curve; the displayed division is not valid. In Q35, a=0a=0a=0 makes both coordinates constant, so no curve slope can be obtained by cancelling aaa.

Concept C10 — The second derivative is the derivative of the slope

f′f'f′ is itself a function: it assigns a tangent slope to each input where the derivative exists. f′′=(f′)′f''=(f')'f′′=(f′)′ measures how that slope changes. It is not (f′)2(f')^2(f′)2.

For y=x2ln⁡xy=x^2\ln xy=x2lnx,

y′=2xln⁡x+x,y′′=2ln⁡x+3(x>0).y'=2x\ln x+x,\qquad \boxed{y''=2\ln x+3}\quad(x>0).y′=2xlnx+x,y′′=2lnx+3​(x>0).

For a composite function F(u(x))F(u(x))F(u(x)),

y′′=F′′(u)(u′)2+F′(u)u′′.\boxed{y''=F''(u)(u')^2+F'(u)u''}.y′′=F′′(u)(u′)2+F′(u)u′′​.

The second term comes from differentiating the inner rate too.

Repeated mixed products: for y=exsin⁡xy=e^x\sin xy=exsinx,

y′=ex(sin⁡x+cos⁡x),y′′=2excos⁡x.y'=e^x(\sin x+\cos x),\qquad y''=2e^x\cos x.y′=ex(sinx+cosx),y′′=2excosx.

So y′′−2y′+2y=0y''-2y'+2y=0y′′−2y′+2y=0. The supplied equation is an identity to check by differentiating twice; it does not require solving a differential equation.

For y=Acos⁡(ln⁡x)+Bsin⁡(ln⁡x)y=A\cos(\ln x)+B\sin(\ln x)y=Acos(lnx)+Bsin(lnx), first write xy′=−Asin⁡(ln⁡x)+Bcos⁡(ln⁡x)xy'=-A\sin(\ln x)+B\cos(\ln x)xy′=−Asin(lnx)+Bcos(lnx). Differentiating this product gives xy′′+y′=−y/xxy''+y'=-y/xxy′′+y′=−y/x, hence x2y′′+xy′+y=0x^2y''+xy'+y=0x2y′′+xy′+y=0.

Recognition clue: multiply away a repeated inner 1/x1/x1/x before a second derivative when that makes the expression shorter.

Concept C11 — Inverse-function slopes are reciprocal at corresponding points

An inverse function swaps the input and output. If b=f(a)b=f(a)b=f(a) and g=f−1g=f^{-1}g=f−1 is the corresponding local inverse, then

g(f(x))=x.g(f(x))=x.g(f(x))=x.

Use the chain rule:

g′(f(x))f′(x)=1⇒g′(b)=1f′(a)(f′(a)≠0).g'(f(x))f'(x)=1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \boxed{g'(b)=\frac1{f'(a)}}\quad(f'(a)\ne0).g′(f(x))f′(x)=1⇒g′(b)=f′(a)1​​(f′(a)=0).

First find which input aaa gives the requested output bbb. Plugging bbb directly into f′f'f′ is usually the wrong point.

For f(x)=x3+x+1f(x)=x^3+x+1f(x)=x3+x+1, f′(x)=3x2+1>0f'(x)=3x^2+1>0f′(x)=3x2+1>0, so fff increases strictly and has one real inverse. Since f(1)=3f(1)=3f(1)=3, g′(3)=1/f′(1)=1/4g'(3)=1/f'(1)=1/4g′(3)=1/f′(1)=1/4. We do not need to solve the cubic inverse explicitly.

The nonzero-derivative condition matters. An inverse may exist even when its derivative is not finite at the corresponding point, as with x3x^3x3 and x1/3x^{1/3}x1/3 at zero.

Concept C12 — Source extension: Rolle and mean value theorems

These theorems are needed for four supplied questions, but are not named in the current official syllabus. Retain them for understanding the source; prioritize the core differentiation and continuity tools first.

Rolle's theorem: if fff is continuous on [a,b][a,b][a,b], differentiable on (a,b)(a,b)(a,b), and f(a)=f(b)f(a)=f(b)f(a)=f(b), then at least one c∈(a,b)c\in(a,b)c∈(a,b) has

f′(c)=0.\boxed{f'(c)=0}.f′(c)=0​.

Equal endpoint heights force at least one horizontal tangent for a curve satisfying those conditions. The statement does not promise a unique ccc.

Read the picture: the two interior turns are both allowed by Rolle's theorem. The vertical shift used in the drawing does not change slopes.

Lagrange's mean value theorem: if fff is continuous on [a,b][a,b][a,b] and differentiable on (a,b)(a,b)(a,b), then some c∈(a,b)c\in(a,b)c∈(a,b) satisfies

f′(c)=f(b)−f(a)b−a.\boxed{f'(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}}.f′(c)=b−af(b)−f(a)​​.

The right side is the endpoint chord's slope, the average change. Some tangent inside has that same slope.

Why the conditions? The continuous graph can reach its extreme heights on the closed interval. If equal endpoints surround a different interior height, an interior maximum or minimum has derivative zero. For the mean value theorem, subtract the chord line and apply Rolle to the resulting equal-endpoint function.

Corners or missing values can break the conclusion. For ∣x∣|x|∣x∣ on [−1,1][-1,1][−1,1], the endpoint heights are equal, but its only potential turning input is a corner with no derivative. Rolle cannot be applied.

An important consequence used in C14: a differentiable function with derivative zero throughout an interval is constant there. Apply the mean value theorem between any two inputs.

Concept C13 — Rational and irrational pieces need branch-limit reasoning

Rational inputs and irrational inputs both occur arbitrarily close to every real number. This is called density; neither set has a small empty neighbourhood around a real point.

Suppose

f(x)={P(x),x rational,Q(x),x irrational,f(x)=\begin{cases}P(x),&x\text{ rational},\\ Q(x),&x\text{ irrational},\end{cases}f(x)={P(x),Q(x),​x rational,x irrational,​

where P,QP,QP,Q are continuous at aaa. Approaching through rational inputs gives P(a)P(a)P(a); approaching through irrational inputs gives Q(a)Q(a)Q(a).

Therefore

f is continuous at a  ⟺  P(a)=Q(a).\boxed{f\text{ is continuous at }a\iff P(a)=Q(a)}.f is continuous at a⟺P(a)=Q(a)​.

Why is matching enough? Both continuous branches then approach the same height; every nearby input uses one of those branches. The actual assigned branch at aaa also has that height.

Read the picture carefully: the dots are illustrative samples. The supporting curves show the two formulas; the actual mixed function is not a connected choice of one curve followed by the other.

For Q33, continuity requires a2=5a−6a^2=5a-6a2=5a−6, giving a=2,3a=2,3a=2,3. Solving the intersection equation is enough; drawing a dense exact graph is neither possible nor necessary.

Concept C14 — Functional equations: derive a local identity, then check all data

A functional equation relates values at different inputs. For

f(x+h)=f(x)f(h),f(x+h)=f(x)f(h),f(x+h)=f(x)f(h),

one nonzero value forces f(0)=1f(0)=1f(0)=1: put h=0h=0h=0. If fff is differentiable at zero,

f′(x)=lim⁡h→0f(x+h)−f(x)h=f(x)lim⁡h→0f(h)−1h=f(x)f′(0).\begin{aligned} f'(x) &=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}h\\ &=f(x)\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(h)-1}h =f(x)f'(0). \end{aligned}f′(x)​=h→0lim​hf(x+h)−f(x)​=f(x)h→0lim​hf(h)−1​=f(x)f′(0).​

This is the useful recognition pattern: the equation turns a derivative at a general input into a derivative at zero.

But check that the remaining numbers are compatible. If f′(0)=3f'(0)=3f′(0)=3, define H(x)=e−3xf(x)H(x)=e^{-3x}f(x)H(x)=e−3xf(x). Product differentiation gives

H′(x)=e−3x(f′(x)−3f(x))=0.H'(x)=e^{-3x}(f'(x)-3f(x))=0.H′(x)=e−3x(f′(x)−3f(x))=0.

Thus HHH is constant, and H(0)=1H(0)=1H(0)=1. Consequently

f(x)=e3x.\boxed{f(x)=e^{3x}}.f(x)=e3x​.

The printed Q34 value f(5)=2f(5)=2f(5)=2 conflicts with f(5)=e15f(5)=e^{15}f(5)=e15. The local substitution f′(5)=3(2)=6f'(5)=3(2)=6f′(5)=3(2)=6 explains the intended option, but it does not create a function satisfying the contradictory givens.

Lesson: a valid intermediate identity is not enough if another given contradicts the function it forces.

Choose the route from the clue

Clue First useful move Why
Piecewise function with a filled value Match left limit, right limit, value Continuity is a height condition
“Differentiable at the join” Continuity first, then side slopes Slope matching cannot repair a jump
Modulus root Inspect local factors A vanishing multiplier may remove the corner
Floor function Locate integer levels and inspect sides Do not count every real input
Oscillation with powers of xxx Check the quotient at zero separately Nearby derivative formulas need not extend
Nested function Name inside and outside Keeps the chain-rule factor
Both base and exponent vary Logarithmic differentiation Both changes contribute
Inverse trig of a multiple-angle pattern Check the principal interval Cancellation outside the branch is false
Parametric second derivative Differentiate the slope and divide by x′x'x′ again The requested variable is xxx, not ttt
Inverse function derivative at bbb Solve f(a)=bf(a)=bf(a)=b first Slopes are reciprocal at corresponding points
Rational/irrational pieces Match branch limits Both input types occur near every point
Functional equation Use a small increment, then audit the data A formal answer may conceal inconsistent givens

This is a teaching aid, not a measured frequency ranking.

Worked solutions to the 35 PDF questions

Try first, then read why the visible clue suggests the method. In a graph question, identify the relevant height, slope or side behaviour before calculating. Every useful second approach remains visible.

Question 1 — Fill the hole at the nearby limiting height

PDF page 48 | MCQ | Notes: C01

Let f(x)=sin⁡3x/xf(x)=\sin3x/xf(x)=sin3x/x for x≠0x\ne0x=0 and f(0)=kf(0)=kf(0)=k. If fff is continuous at x=0x=0x=0, then kkk equals

  • (a) 111
  • (b) 13\dfrac1331​
  • (c) 333
  • (d) 000

f(x)=3sin⁡3x3x⟶3.f(x)=3\frac{\sin3x}{3x}\longrightarrow3.f(x)=33xsin3x​⟶3.

So the assigned value must be k=3\boxed{k=3}k=3​, option (c).

Why not substitute zero in the fraction? It gives 0/00/00/0; it does not define f(0)f(0)f(0). The separately assigned kkk must match the limit.

Another possible approach: sin⁡3x=3x+O(x3)\sin3x=3x+O(x^3)sin3x=3x+O(x3) gives f(x)=3+O(x2)→3f(x)=3+O(x^2)\to3f(x)=3+O(x2)→3.

Question 3 — Count genuine slope changes at modulus points

PDF page 48 | Numerical value | Notes: C06

The number of points at which f(x)=∣x∣+∣x−1∣+∣x−2∣+∣x−3∣f(x)=|x|+|x-1|+|x-2|+|x-3|f(x)=∣x∣+∣x−1∣+∣x−2∣+∣x−3∣ is not differentiable is ____.

Each modulus changes slope where its inside becomes zero. The candidates are 0,1,2,30,1,2,30,1,2,3. Away from those inputs all signs are fixed, so the sum is a straight-line expression locally.

As xxx crosses one candidate, exactly one term changes slope from −1-1−1 to 111. The other terms have the same slope on both sides of that candidate. The total slope therefore jumps by 222.

Explicitly, the slopes are

−4, −2, 0, 2, 4-4,\ -2,\ 0,\ 2,\ 4−4, −2, 0, 2, 4

on (−∞,0),(0,1),(1,2),(2,3),(3,∞)(-\infty,0),(0,1),(1,2),(2,3),(3,\infty)(−∞,0),(0,1),(1,2),(2,3),(3,∞). Thus all four candidates are genuine corners: 4\boxed{4}4​.

Another possible approach: form the left and right derivative at each candidate directly. This gives the same four slope jumps. Counting zeros alone would need more care if negative weights or vanishing multipliers could cancel a corner.

Question 4 — A joined graph can still have two slopes

PDF page 48 | MCQ | Notes: C02

Statement I: f(x)=∣x∣f(x)=|x|f(x)=∣x∣ is continuous at x=0x=0x=0.

Statement II: f(x)=∣x∣f(x)=|x|f(x)=∣x∣ is differentiable at x=0x=0x=0. Choose the correct option.

  • (b) Statement I is true but Statement II is false
  • (c) Statement I is false but Statement II is true
  • (d) Both Statement I and Statement II are false

Separate height from slope. The value is f(0)=0f(0)=0f(0)=0 and ∣x∣→0|x|\to0∣x∣→0, so Statement I is true.

The derivative quotient is

∣h∣−0h={−1,h<0,1,h>0.\frac{|h|-0}{h} =\begin{cases}-1,&h<0,\\1,&h>0.\end{cases}h∣h∣−0​={−1,1,​h<0,h>0.​

The left and right slopes differ, so Statement II is false. The answer is option (b)\boxed{\text{option (b)}}option (b)​.

Another possible view: write the two straight-line pieces as −x-x−x for x<0x<0x<0 and xxx for x>0x>0x>0. Their slopes are −1-1−1 and 111. A joined graph need not have a unique tangent.

PDF page 48 | Numerical value | Notes: C05

If ddx ⁣[sin⁡−1 ⁣(2x1−x2)]=k ddx[sin⁡−1x]\dfrac{d}{dx}\!\left[\sin^{-1}\!\left(2x\sqrt{1-x^2}\right)\right]=k\,\dfrac{d}{dx}[\sin^{-1}x]dxd​[sin−1(2x1−x2​)]=kdxd​[sin−1x] for ∣x∣<1/2|x|<1/\sqrt2∣x∣<1/2​, then k=k=k= ____.

2x1−x2=2sin⁡θcos⁡θ=sin⁡2θ.2x\sqrt{1-x^2}=2\sin\theta\cos\theta=\sin2\theta.2x1−x2​=2sinθcosθ=sin2θ.

Now 2θ∈(−π/2,π/2)2\theta\in(-\pi/2,\pi/2)2θ∈(−π/2,π/2), the principal arcsine interval, so

2(1−2x2)1−x21−4x2(1−x2)=2(1−2x2)1−x2∣1−2x2∣.\frac{2(1-2x^2)} {\sqrt{1-x^2}\sqrt{1-4x^2(1-x^2)}} =\frac{2(1-2x^2)} {\sqrt{1-x^2}|1-2x^2|}.1−x2​1−4x2(1−x2)​2(1−2x2)​=1−x2​∣1−2x2∣2(1−2x2)​.

Question 6 — Both the base and the exponent depend on x

PDF page 48 | MCQ | Notes: C08

If y=xxy=x^xy=xx for x>0x>0x>0, then dydx\dfrac{dy}{dx}dxdy​ at x=2x=2x=2 is

Coverage and source notes

All 353535 supplied questions appear in order: 252525 MCQs and 101010 numerical-value questions. All intended source answers have been independently checked, with these qualifications:

  • Q34's formal local calculation gives the keyed 666, but the complete data contradict the forced exponential. There is no such differentiable real function.
  • Q35's slope applies for a≠0a\ne0a=0. The zero-scale case is a fixed point.
  • Q7, Q8, Q26 and Q31 are retained mean-value-theorem source extensions, not labelled as new core syllabus requirements.
  • The printed inverse-trig restrictions and natural log domains are retained. A finite sample plot is never used to prove dense-input or infinitely oscillating behaviour.

Its separate Limits and Derivatives category and ExamSIDE's LCD/Differentiation split use different boundaries. No category datasets were merged.
